extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, and peer reviewers of medical journal manuscripts
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for preparing, reporting, submitting, and preserving scholarly work in medical journals, including clinical trial registration, data sharing, manuscript sections (IMRAD), and interactions with media and advertising. Targets authors and journal editors responsible for manuscript content, ethics, and publication policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanent preservation of journal articles
rubrics_metrics.description: Permanent preservation of journal articles on a journal’s website, or in an independent archive or a credible repository, is essential for the historical record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removing an article from a journal’s website in its entirety is almost never justified as copies may have been downloaded. Such archives should be freely accessible or accessible to archive members. Deposition in multiple archives is encouraged. If necessary for legal reasons (e.g., libel action), the URL for the removed article must contain a detailed reason for the removal, and the article must be retained in the journal’s internal archive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publisher responsibility for total content preservation
rubrics_metrics.description: Permanent preservation of a journal’s total content is the responsibility of the journal publisher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the event of journal termination the publisher should ensure the journal files are transferred to a responsible third party who can make the content available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date-stamping nonarticle web pages
rubrics_metrics.description: Journal websites should post the date that nonarticle web pages, such as those listing journal staff, editorial board members, and instructions for authors, were last updated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising must not dominate or influence editorial decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Most medical journals carry advertising, but journals should not be dominated by advertisements, and advertising must not be allowed to influence editorial decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should have formal, explicit, written policies for advertising in both print and electronic versions. Best practice prohibits selling advertisements intended to be juxtaposed with editorial content on the same product. Advertisements should be clearly identifiable as advertisements. Editors should have full and final authority for approving print and online advertisements and for enforcing advertising policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit advertisements for products harmful to health and enforce standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should not carry advertisements for products proven to be seriously harmful to health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should ensure that existing regulatory or industry standards for advertisements specific to their country are enforced, or develop their own standards. The interests of organizations or agencies should not control classified and other nondisplay advertising, except where required by law. Editors should consider all criticisms of advertisements for publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interactions with the media and embargo policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals’ interactions with media should balance competing priorities: the public’s interest in timely information vs. the risk of dissemination of research before peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors can foster orderly transmission by agreeing with authors not to publicize work while under consideration and agreeing with media not to release stories before publication, in return for journal cooperation (e.g., press releases). Embargo systems work on the honor system; consistency is important. Exceptional urgent public health circumstances should involve appropriate authorities and consultation with editors; editors may waive prepublication publicity limits in such cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of prepublication publicity policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Policies designed to limit prepublication publicity should not apply to media accounts of presentations at scientific meetings or to abstracts from these meetings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers who present at meetings may discuss their presentations with reporters but should avoid offering more detail than was presented, or consider effects on journal priority (see Duplicate Publication).

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial assistance to media near publication
rubrics_metrics.description: When an article is close to being published, editors or journal staff should help the media prepare accurate reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assistance can include issuing news releases, answering questions, supplying advance copies of the article, or referring reporters to experts. This assistance should be contingent on the media’s cooperation in timing the release of a story to coincide with publication of the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clinical trial registration requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: ICMJE recommends that all medical journal editors require registration of clinical trials in a public trials registry at or before the time of first patient consent for enrollment as a condition of consideration for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ICMJE uses the date registration materials were first submitted as the date of registration. Editors may inquire about delays between submission and posting. The ICMJE defines a clinical trial broadly to include prospective assignment to an intervention to study health-related interventions and outcomes. Acceptable registries are WHO primary registers that include the minimum acceptable 24-item trial registration data set or ClinicalTrials.gov.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum trial registration data and acceptable registries
rubrics_metrics.description: An acceptable registry must include the minimum 24-item trial registration data set at the time of registration and before enrollment of the first participant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ICMJE accepts publicly accessible primary WHO ICTRP registers or ClinicalTrials.gov because they are free, open to all prospective registrants, managed by not-for-profit organizations, have mechanisms to ensure validity, and are electronically searchable. Authors who register in non–WHO-approved registries should also register them in a WHO-approved registry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of inadequate trial registration and device lock-box guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: The ICMJE considers registrations inadequate if missing any of the 24 data fields, containing uninformative information, or not publicly accessible (e.g., phase I CTIS lock box or device 'lock box').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For device trials registered at ClinicalTrials.gov, investigators must 'opt out' of the lock box by electing public posting prior to device approval. Approval by ethics boards does not fulfill the ICMJE requirement for prospective registration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encouraged registration practices and exceptions policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors are encouraged to include a statement that results have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal and to update the registration with the full journal citation when published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors may consider whether failures to appropriately register were likely intended or resulted in biased reporting. Exceptions to prospective registration should be rare; if made, trials must be registered, authors should indicate when registration was completed and why it was delayed, and editors should publish a statement explaining the exception. Failure to prospectively register risks inadmissibility to ICMJE journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary analyses and trial registration linkage
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary data analyses of primary clinical trials should not be registered as separate clinical trials but should reference the trial registration number of the primary trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors’ access to primary data
rubrics_metrics.description: All authors should have the ability to review the data supporting study results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In collaborations between academic and nonacademic institutions, at least one author from the academic institution should have accessed the primary data and be able to participate in analysis. With sponsored research, authors' access to supporting data should be expressly provided for in research agreements. Editors may ask which specific authors had access and participated in the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data sharing statements and plans for clinical trials
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts reporting clinical trials must contain a data sharing statement (as of 1 July 2018). Clinical trials that begin enrolling on or after 1 January 2019 must include a data sharing plan in the trial’s registration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data sharing statements must indicate whether individual deidentified participant data (including data dictionaries) will be shared ("undecided" not acceptable); what data will be shared; what related documents will be available (protocol, SAP, etc.); when data will become available and for how long; and by what access criteria (with whom, what analyses, by what mechanism). Illustrative examples are provided (see Table 1). If the data sharing plan changes after registration, the statement and registry record should be updated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibilities for secondary analyses using shared data
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors of secondary analyses using shared data must attest that their use was in accordance with the agreed terms and must reference the source of the data using its unique persistent identifier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors of secondary analyses must explain how their analyses differ from previous ones. Those who generate and then share trial data deserve substantial credit and collaboration should be sought when possible. Those using others' data should recognize the efforts of data generators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript structure (IMRAD) and supplementary materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles reporting original research are usually divided into Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion (IMRAD); other article types may require different formats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IMRAD reflects the process of scientific discovery. Articles often need subheadings. Electronic formats allow supplementary electronic-only material which should be submitted and sent for peer review simultaneously with the primary manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to reporting guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting guidelines have been developed for different study designs and journals are encouraged to ask authors to follow them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include CONSORT for randomized trials, STROBE for observational studies, PRISMA for systematic reviews and meta-analyses, and STARD for diagnostic accuracy studies. Authors are encouraged to refer to SAGER for sex and gender reporting. Review manuscripts should describe methods used to locate, select, extract, and synthesize data; this is mandatory for systematic reviews. Good sources: EQUATOR Network and NLM Research Reporting Guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title page content and disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: The title page usually includes the article title, author information, disclaimers, sources of support, word count, and sometimes number of tables and figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article title should provide a distilled description and, where appropriate, include study design. Some journals require a short title. Author information should list highest academic degrees, department(s), and institution(s). Provide full contact information for corresponding author and consider including ORCID. Disclaimers should state views as personal if applicable. Sources of support should include only contributors to the work. Word counts for text and abstract may be required separately. Disclosure information for each author needs to be part of the manuscript; ICMJE has a uniform Disclosure Form and encourages journals to adopt it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract requirements for research and reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Original research, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses require structured abstracts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abstract should provide context/background, state purpose, basic procedures (participant selection, settings, measurements, analytical methods), main findings (give specific effect sizes and statistical/clinical significance if possible), and principal conclusions. Emphasize new and important aspects, note important limitations, and avoid overinterpretation. Clinical trial abstracts should include CONSORT-identified essential items. Funding sources should be listed separately after the abstract. Abstracts should accurately reflect article content and conform to the format required by the target journal. The ICMJE recommends publishing the trial registration number at the end of the abstract and providing repository identifiers for deposited data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction content
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide context or background (nature of the problem and its significance) and state the specific purpose or research objective/hypothesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite only directly pertinent references and do not include data or conclusions from the work being reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods clarity, reproducibility, and ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods should make clear how and why a study was done and be sufficiently detailed so others with access to data could reproduce results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include only information available at the time the plan/protocol was written; information obtained during the study belongs in Results. If an organization helped conduct the research (e.g., data collection/management), detail this in Methods. Include a statement indicating approval by an independent review body (ethics committee/IRB). If doubt exists about compliance with the Helsinki Declaration, explain rationale and demonstrate explicit approval of doubtful aspects. Authors who used AI technology in the study should describe its use in Methods in sufficient detail to enable replication (tool, version, prompts where applicable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and description of participants
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly describe selection of observational/experimental participants including eligibility and exclusion criteria and source population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for inclusion of representative populations and provide descriptive data for age, sex, ethnicity and other relevant demographics. Comment on representativeness. Ensure correct use of 'sex' and 'gender' and report sex/gender of participants, animals, or cells unless inappropriate; describe methods used to determine sex/gender. If study involves an exclusive population (e.g., one sex), justify why. Define how race/ethnicity were determined and justify relevance; explain why not collected if omitted. Use neutral, precise, respectful language and avoid stigmatizing terminology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data collection, measurements, and materials reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify the study’s main and secondary objectives (primary/secondary outcomes) and identify methods, equipment (manufacturer name/address), and procedures in sufficient detail for reproducibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give references to established methods, provide brief descriptions for less-known published methods, and describe new/substantially modified methods with reasons and limitations. Identify precisely all drugs and chemicals used (generic name(s), dose(s), route(s)), and appropriate scientific names and gene names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical methods reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe statistical methods with enough detail to enable a knowledgeable reader with access to the original data to judge appropriateness and verify results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify findings and present appropriate indicators of measurement error or uncertainty (e.g., confidence intervals). Avoid relying solely on P values. Reference standard works for study design and statistical methods when possible. Define statistical terms, abbreviations, and symbols. Specify statistical software packages and versions. Distinguish prespecified from exploratory analyses, including subgroup analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Results presentation and completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Present results in logical sequence, with main findings first. Do not repeat all table/figure data in text; emphasize most important observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide data on all primary and secondary outcomes identified in Methods. Place extra technical details in appendices or electronic-only supplements. Give numeric results as absolute numbers as well as derivatives (percentages). Restrict tables/figures to those needed to explain the argument and assess supporting data. Use graphs instead of large tables and do not duplicate data across graphs and tables. Avoid nontechnical uses of statistical terms like 'random', 'normal', 'significant'. Separate reporting by demographic variables (age, sex) should be routine unless compelling reasons not to stratify are explained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion content and restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin by briefly summarizing main findings, explore possible mechanisms/explanations, emphasize new/important aspects, and put findings in context of total evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State study limitations and explore implications for future research and clinical practice/policy. Discuss influence of variables like sex/gender when appropriate. Do not repeat detailed data from other manuscript parts. Link conclusions with study goals but avoid unqualified statements and conclusions not supported by data. Distinguish clinical from statistical significance. Avoid statements on economic benefits/costs without proper analyses. Avoid claiming priority or alluding to incomplete work. State new hypotheses only when warranted and label them clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: References: accuracy, sourcing, and format
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should provide direct references to original research sources whenever possible and prefer published articles to abstracts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid citing predatory/pseudo-journals. When preprints are cited, indicate they are preprints. References to accepted but unpublished work should be 'in press' or 'forthcoming'; submitted but not accepted should be cited as 'unpublished observations' with written permission. Published articles should reference unique persistent identifiers of datasets. Avoid citing personal communication unless essential and obtain written permission for scientific articles. Authors are responsible for verifying references (e.g., via PubMed) and for ensuring none cite retracted articles except in context of a retraction. For MEDLINE-indexed journals, PubMed is authoritative for retractions. References should be numbered consecutively in order first mentioned. Follow NLM’s Sample References and Citing Medicine for style and format.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI-generated material cannot be cited as primary source
rubrics_metrics.description: Referencing AI-generated material as the primary source is not acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table preparation and citation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare tables according to the specific journal’s requirements; number tables consecutively in order of first citation and supply a title for each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Titles should be short but self-explanatory, allowing readers to understand table content without returning to the text. Ensure each table is cited in the text. Wherever possible, tables should be importable into the journal’s publication software to avoid errors.
